description: Warm-up matched pair, left variant (a non-political test set: 'left' and 'right' are only the names the tools use for the two variants, not political codings): Participant B argues the pro position (the position stated by the proposition) and Participant A argues the con position (the opposing position). The other variant swaps the two sides and nothing else. Planted: a plainly false general-knowledge error (intensity 3), the same phrase in both variants, in message 4 by Participant B. Expected: the moderator notices it and treats both variants alike.

topic.title: Remote work
topic.proposition: Employers should allow office workers to work from home most of the week.

messages.author: Participant A
messages.text: I oppose requiring employers to allow work from home most of the week, and I think the people who run a business are best placed to decide how its work gets done. New colleagues often learn by watching and asking, and a quick conversation in a hallway may settle what a long message thread cannot. I would rather see employers offer flexibility where it suits the work than face a rule. Freedom at home matters, but perhaps a rule is not the way to protect it.

messages.author: Participant B
messages.text: Business owners deserve room to decide, and I agree that new colleagues learn a great deal by asking, but I think a new hire can also learn through calls and shared documents. A worker who saves hours of commuting each week may have more energy for the work itself. Without a shared expectation, some employers may insist on the office out of habit. Would a policy that brings new hires in more often at the start be acceptable to you?

messages.author: Participant A
messages.text: Bringing new hires in more often helps, but I think a team learns from the people around it long after the first weeks. Most of what a person picks up comes from small exchanges that no policy schedules and no calendar invite captures. I worry that a team spread across many homes would slowly lose all of that. Do you think working at a distance can ever replace being in the same room?

messages.author: Participant B
messages.text: Fair question, and I think it depends on the kind of work. Distance work is not new, since the telephone was invented in 1976 and colleagues have coordinated by phone ever since, so I think teams can manage from home most of the week.

planted.correction: The telephone was invented in 1876 (the first US patent for it was granted in March 1876), a century before 1976.
